area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what changes when a stall happens with the power on, fly a power-on stall from the right seat while you explain it, and teach it: set it up safely, brief and demonstrate it, handle a learner who freezes or overcontrols, and spot and fix the common errors.
why: Power-on stalls rehearse the departure accident: a nose pitched too high right after takeoff, in a climbing turn, or while trying to clear an obstacle [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Many stall/spin accidents have happened in takeoff and climbout, especially during go-arounds [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]], and 60 percent of the stall/spin accidents in the NTSB data the AIH cites happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. As the instructor you set this stall up at high power and a high nose, with a learner who may not be ready for the yaw, so how you brief, guard and demonstrate it decides whether the lesson is safe and useful.

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a straight-ahead power-on stall. As the nose comes up through the climb attitude at full power, the ball slides right, the nose drifts left, and the learner says nothing. At the break the left wing drops. Which force was building, what should the learner's feet have been doing, and what is the one thing you will say on the next attempt, before the nose comes up, to stop this happening again?

key_terms.def: Also called a departure stall: practiced to simulate takeoff and climbout conditions and configuration [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]].
Slowing to normal lift-off speed before adding power, so the nose is not held excessively high for a long time before the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Power-on stalls are normally practiced in takeoff configuration and also clean, with flaps and gear up, to cover every takeoff and climb configuration [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
The engine and propeller turn one way, so the airplane tends to roll the other way, to the left with a clockwise propeller [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
The corkscrew of air from the propeller striking the vertical fin. It is compact and strong at high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in approaches to power-on stalls [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
At a high AOA the downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite, moving the center of thrust right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
A force on the spinning propeller acts 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation, so a pitch change gives a yaw and a yaw gives a pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
A stall from adding full power for a go-around with nose-up trim set and no firm control of pitch; the nose rises sharply and turns left [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
An uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex with raised heart rate and blood pressure, set off by a sudden, intense event that violates expectations [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
VX gives the greatest altitude gain over a given distance; VY the greatest gain per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
An aggravated stall: at least one wing past the critical AOA with sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

chunks.title: What changes when the power is on

body.p: Start the brief with the purpose. Power-on stall recoveries are practiced from straight climbs and climbing turns of 15 to 20 degrees of bank, so the pilot learns to recognize an accidental stall during takeoff, a go-around, a climb, or an attempt to clear an obstacle [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

The general stall material (AOA, the critical AOA, sight, sound and feel, and the recovery template) is in the Power-Off Stalls lesson (AI.X.C). Here we cover only what is different with the power on, which is what your learner needs to hear:

bullets: The accident it rehearses: departure stalls. Many stall/spin accidents happened in takeoff and climbout, particularly go-arounds, with nose-high trim, premature flap retraction and short-field takeoffs among the causes [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]].

Configuration: normally takeoff configuration, but also clean, flaps and gear up, so every takeoff and climb configuration gets practiced [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. On the checkride the evaluator picks takeoff, departure or cruise configuration (AI.X.D.S3).

Power: the AFH uses maximum power for takeoff stall practice, or less in some airplanes to prevent an excessively high pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The CFI ACS asks for no less than 65 percent power (AI.X.D.S4).
Entry speed: slow to normal lift-off speed first, then add power, to avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time before the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Yaw: as the speed decays the elevator comes progressively further back while right rudder is added, all the way to the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Recovery: since the throttle is already at climb power, the power step may just mean confirming the setting [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

callout.text: CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task D: "In some high-performance airplanes, the power setting may have to be reduced below the ACS guidelines power setting to prevent pitch attitudes greater than 30° nose up." The same note says the evaluation "does not mandate a predetermined value for altitude loss and does not mandate maintaining altitude during recovery."

Application: open the ground lesson with a question, not a lecture. 'Where on a normal flight are you nose high, slow and at full power?' A learner who answers 'go-around, short-field takeoff, climbing turn after takeoff' has just written your lesson objective.

check.q: Why does the AFH have the pilot slow to lift-off speed before setting takeoff or climb power for a power-on stall?
check.a: To avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time before the airplane stalls [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

chunks.title: Aerodynamics: what power changes and what it does not

body.p: The wing does not care about the throttle. A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, whatever its airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]], and the critical AOA can be exceeded at any power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Teach K2 as the list of things power moves around that fixed AOA:

head: Factor
With the power on
Source
rows: Angle of attack
Still the only thing that stalls the wing; the picture out the window is much higher, but the critical AOA is the same
Airspeed
Propeller slipstream lowers the power-on stall speed. In the PHAK sample airplane, gear and flaps up, wings level: 54 knots power on, 65 knots power off
Load factor
A stall from an unaccelerated straight climb adds no load factor; a bank or an abrupt pull adds G and raises the stall speed
Power setting
More slipstream over the tail raises the nose more than desired in many airplanes, and the left-turning tendencies grow
Weight
More weight needs a higher AOA for the extra lift, so the stall speed rises
Center of gravity
Aft CG: less elevator force to reach a high AOA, easier inadvertent entry and, if a spin starts, a possible flat spin. Forward CG: the stalling AOA comes at a higher airspeed
Airplane attitude
Not a reliable stall cue, since the airplane can stall in any attitude. Some light-sport makers limit pitch to 30 degrees in power-on stalls
Yaw effects
Engine and propeller effects yaw the airplane; yaw at or beyond the stall is what turns it into a spin

body.p: Configuration: flaps generally lower the stall speed [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]], so a takeoff-flap stall and a clean stall come at different speeds and attitudes. The airspeed indicator arcs mark power-off stall speeds [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]]. Application: at full power the stall can come below the bottom of the arc, which surprises learners who watch the airspeed indicator.

Climbing turns: with constant power, the same pitch and airspeed cannot be held in a bank, extra back pressure is needed, and medium or steep banks degrade the climb or remove it [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. That is why the turning power-off and power-on stalls feel different: the turning power-on stall combines high power, bank and a nose-high attitude.

callout.text: Application: on the whiteboard, draw the same wing at the same AOA twice, once on a descending path and once on a steep climbing path. The nose picture is very different; the AOA is not. Learners who 'feel' the stall by pitch alone are the ones who get surprised by it.

check.q: A learner says, 'Power-on stalls happen at a higher angle of attack because the nose is so much higher.' How do you correct this?
check.a: The critical AOA is the same for a given airplane regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]; the attitude is higher, and attitude is not a reliable stall cue [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

body.p: To the pilot, 'torque' is really four elements [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]]. A power-on stall stacks all four at once, which is why it is the best place to teach rudder:

head: Element
What it does
Why it peaks in a power-on stall
rows: Torque reaction
Rolls the airplane left, opposite a clockwise propeller [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Full power
Spiraling slipstream
Strikes the vertical fin and yaws the nose; also gives a rolling moment to the right [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
The PHAK names high propeller speed and low forward speed, 'as in the takeoffs and approaches to power-on stalls' [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Gyroscopic precession
A pitch change gives a yaw, and a yaw gives a pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
Abrupt pitch changes at the entry and in the recovery
P-factor
The downward blade's bigger bite moves the thrust right and yaws the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
High AOA: nose high and slow

body.p: Builders set the fixes for torque to work at cruise speed, where the airplane spends most of its time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. At climb power and low speed the pilot makes up the rest with right rudder. In the climb, torque and P-factor roll and yaw the airplane left, countered with right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. In the power-on stall entry the right rudder keeps growing as the speed decays [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

Teach it before the first stall. AC 61-67C's slow flight plan has you note the left-turning tendency, emphasize the right rudder needed to center the ball and hold heading, then release the rudder and have the learner watch the left yaw [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]]. A learner who has seen the yaw at slow flight power will believe your rudder brief at full power.

The rudder job continues in the recovery. The AFH power-on recovery is: reduce the AOA until the stall warning stops, level the wings with ailerons, coordinate with rudder, and confirm the power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The recovery template adds that the pilot must proactively cancel yaw with the rudder so the stall does not progress into a spin, and use rudder and elevator to stop any yawing motion as power is applied [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. As the speed builds, the slipstream spiral elongates and weakens [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]], and P-factor shrinks as the propeller shaft lines up with the moving air [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]], so the right rudder needed at the stall will not stay the same. Application: the PHAK shows precession only for raising the tail (left yaw) [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]; a brisk push may give a brief yaw too, so coach "fly the ball", not "hold right rudder".

callout.text: These elements vary in value from one phase of flight to the next and between airframes, engines and propellers; the pilot must use the controls to compensate for whichever is strongest at the time [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

check.q: Which of the four left-turning elements does the PHAK tie by name to the approach to a power-on stall, and why there?
check.a: The spiraling slipstream. At high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in takeoffs and approaches to power-on stalls, the spiral is compact and pushes hard on the vertical tail [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

chunks.title: Stall characteristics and cues at high power

body.p: Stall behavior depends on the design: geometry, CG, wing design and high-lift devices [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Most trainers stall root first, so the ailerons keep some effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. With the power on the stall is usually more obvious than with it off: the buffeting and shaking are less noticeable in a power-off stall than in a power-on stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Teach the cues as they appear at full power (AI.X.D.S7):

bullets: Feel: control pressures lighten and response slows [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]; just before the stall, buffeting, uncontrollable pitching or vibration may begin [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. In the entry the learner also feels the elevator coming further back and the right rudder growing [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

Sound: the sound of the air along the airframe changes [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], and with a fixed-pitch propeller the RPM may drop approaching a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Application: full power is loud, so make the learner listen for the horn and watch the tachometer.
Sight: the nose is far above the horizon, but vision is not foolproof since the airplane can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

Full stall: an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot readily be stopped, perhaps with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. If incorrect rudder use created the yaw, the pilot may not know the critical AOA is exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: Wing drop. If a wing rolls off and the learner uses aileron to lift it, the down aileron raises that tip's AOA and can deepen the stall and the roll; reduce the AOA before rolling [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Range and limitations of stall warning indicators (R2):

bullets: The rule: a clear and distinctive stall warning with sufficient margin to prevent inadvertent stalling [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. It may be aerodynamic buffet rather than a device, and many vintage, light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Margin: many devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]], a typical figure, not a promise for your airplane.
Failure: a stall warning system may fail, so other cues must be used: aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority, or inability to arrest a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Contamination: in some icing conditions the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].
AOA indicators: limited by calibration, unheated probes or vanes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

callout.text: Application: on your first demonstration, name each cue out loud as it appears: 'Back pressure growing, right foot working, buffet, horn, and there is the break.' The learner hears the order the cues come in before having to find them alone.

check.q: At the break of a power-on stall the left wing drops and your learner reaches for right aileron first. What does the AFH say that aileron can do?
check.a: The down aileron on the low wing raises its AOA and can deepen the stall at that tip, rolling the airplane further; reduce the AOA before rolling level [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

chunks.title: Stall warnings and stall traps on real departures

body.p: Stall warnings during normal operations (R3). When a stall indicator appears, the recovery should be instinctive unless a full stall is being practiced on purpose; the AC's preliminary fixes are to add power, lower the nose and/or decrease the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Application: on a departure the power is already in, so the fix left is the nose and the bank. Teach every horn after lift-off as an AOA problem.
Factors and situations that lead to a power-on stall, and how to prevent each (K4, R1):

head: Situation
How it leads to a stall
Prevention to teach
rows: Go-around with nose-up trim
Full power raises the nose and yaws left; letting the nose rise too early can mean an unrecoverable stall at low altitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Considerable forward pressure, right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Short-field takeoff
Pulling off early or climbing too steeply: the airplane settles back or hits obstacles, and below VX the climb stays flat [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Rotate to the VX attitude at or near VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Climb at VX
In some airplanes a 5-knot error costs a lot of climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Precise airspeed, not a higher nose
Flap retraction
Raising them all at once can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; premature retraction is a known causal factor [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]
Flaps up in increments once stable at VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]
Climbing turn after takeoff
More back pressure is needed, and medium or steep banks degrade or end the climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Shallow banks during climbs [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Lift-off in ground effect
Under high density altitude, high temperature or maximum weight the airplane may lift off but not climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]
Take off at the recommended speed under marginal conditions [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]
Preoccupation in the climb
Changing configuration or trim, avoiding traffic or clearing obstacles can set up a stall/spin [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Fly first; brief tasks before takeoff

body.p: The road to a spin and loss of control (R1). AC 61-67C calls a go-around or short-field takeoff, at a high pitch attitude, high power and low airspeed, a classic place for P-factor to play a role in a stall/spin accident. Too little or too much rudder leaves the airplane uncoordinated, the airspeed indicator and altimeter become unreliable, and the stall warning may be the first clue; without a prompt recovery a spin is more likely [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

callout.text: Single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics must not have a tendency to inadvertently depart controlled flight [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]], yet mishandled controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can still spin even reluctant airplanes [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: Why does AC 61-67C single out the go-around and the short-field takeoff as classic settings for a P-factor stall/spin?
check.a: Both put the airplane at a high pitch attitude, high power and low airspeed; wrong rudder makes the flight uncoordinated, the pitot-static instruments unreliable, and a spin more likely if recovery is not prompt [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

chunks.title: Recovering when the power is already in

body.p: The fundamentals are the same as in AI.X.C: the most important action in an impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA, and pilots who put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A power-on stall makes that trap easier, because the learner already has full power and may believe power alone will fly them out. It will not: adding power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
What is different in the power-on recovery (R4):

bullets: Nose: apply as much nose-down input as needed to eliminate the stall warning [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Every airplane needs a different amount, and too much forward pressure can hinder recovery with a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Wings and yaw: level with ailerons and coordinate with rudder [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], canceling yaw so the stall does not become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Power: the throttle is already at climb power, so this step may be confirming the setting [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

Speed: nose low at full power builds speed fast. Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and the airspeed indicator and tachometer must never reach their high-speed red lines in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Throttle: with sufficient airspeed and control effectiveness, return the throttle to the appropriate setting as you rejoin the desired flightpath [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: After the recovery (S9, S10). VX gives the most altitude over a distance, VY the most per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Configure as the manufacturer recommends (AI.X.D.S9). The AFH short-field climb is a good model: gear and flaps stay put until clear of obstacles and stable at VY, then the flaps come up in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. To return to the assigned altitude, start the level-off at about 10 percent of the climb rate [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] (AI.X.D.S10).

callout.text: Power is already in, so the cure is the nose: unload, level, ball centered, confirm power, then climb at VX or VY.

Application: before the first full stall, have the learner say the recovery out loud on the ground with their hands on an imaginary yoke and throttle. Listen for 'add power' as the first word; if you hear it, fix it on the ground.

check.q: After a power-on stall recovery the nose is low, the throttle is still full and the airspeed is climbing fast. Which listed error is building, and what limit does AC 61-67C give?
check.a: Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; neither the airspeed indicator nor the tachometer should reach its high-speed red line in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

chunks.title: Secondary, accelerated, elevator trim and cross-control stalls

body.p: Each of these is a power-on stall gone wrong in a particular way. For certification the secondary, cross-control and elevator trim stalls are demonstration-only maneuvers that only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X: "The flight instructor normally demonstrates stall Tasks F, G, and H to learners for the purposes of familiarization and stall/spin awareness." Those are Task F (cross-controlled stall), Task G (elevator trim stall) and Task H (secondary stall). The same note says the evaluator chooses impending or full in the other stall Tasks, except Task H, "where a full stall occurs", and Task E (accelerated), "where the recovery occurs at the first indication".

bullets: Secondary stalls: a stall after a recovery, when the AOA was not reduced enough or the pilot tried to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], or rushed the recovery before flying speed returned [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. The full-power trap: the learner hears the engine and thinks the stall is over. Fix: do the recovery again [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Accelerated stalls: any stall above 1 G, at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Pulling too fast during a power-on stall entry causes one [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. They tend to be more aggressive and can surprise an inexperienced pilot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Elevator trim stalls: full power for a go-around with nose-up approach trim. Propwash over the tail plus the trim make the nose rise sharply and turn left; forward pressure before the stall, then retrim. Taken to a full stall it needs a significant nose-down attitude and altitude loss [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task G: "The applicant and evaluator must brief the recovery prior to stall execution."

Cross-control stalls: the critical AOA exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other; little warning, a sudden bank change and possibly a roll toward inverted [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A spin from crossed controls usually rotates in the direction of the rudder; in a skid with aileron and rudder the same way, rotation follows the controls; in a slip it usually goes opposite the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

body.p: AC 61-67C gives you the elevator trim stall as a training demonstration: trimmed descent in the landing approach configuration, go-around with full power holding only light elevator and right rudder, let the nose pitch up and torque swerve the airplane left, then recover at the first indication to a normal climbing pitch attitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]] [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

callout.text: If a power-on stall becomes a spin, the power must come off. AC 61-67C's first step for an upright spin is to close the throttle completely [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]; the POH technique takes precedence [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Some light-sport airplanes enter spins quickly and aggressively when aggressive pitch is combined with uncoordinated rudder [[24:347|AFH 17-13]].

check.q: A power-on stall develops into an incipient spin. What does AC 61-67C list as the first step of an upright spin recovery, and why does it matter more here than after a power-off stall?
check.a: Close the throttle completely to eliminate power and minimize altitude loss [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. In a power-on stall the throttle is at full power, so the learner must actively pull it back; follow the POH [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

chunks.title: Environment: density altitude, turbulence and microbursts

body.p: Effect of environmental elements on performance in a power-on stall (R6):

bullets: High density altitude: reduces engine and propeller performance, lengthens the takeoff roll and cuts climb performance [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Normally aspirated engines lose power as altitude increases [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. Indicated stall speed hardly changes [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. Application: at a high practice altitude on a hot day, full throttle may give you less than you briefed, so check the POH power table before you promise 65 percent.

Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can raise the AOA suddenly and stall the airplane at a significantly higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Application: in a nose-high entry, a gust can bring the break earlier than the learner expects.

Microbursts: on takeoff the airplane may meet a performance-increasing headwind, then downdrafts, then a rapidly increasing tailwind that can put it into the terrain [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. In the accidents studied, the takeoff looked normal for about 5 seconds after lift-off and the airplane crashed about 20 seconds after lift-off [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]; crews reduced pitch to regain trim speed and lost altitude [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].

callout.text: Some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Teach avoidance: do not depart under a thunderstorm or a heavy rain shaft.

check.q: On a hot, high day your learner's POH shows the stall speeds unchanged in indicated airspeed. What has changed that matters for a power-on stall lesson?
check.a: The engine and propeller make less power and climb performance drops [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]], while indicated stall speed stays about the same [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. The airplane may not reach the briefed power or climb.

chunks.title: Clearing, blind spots, distractions and orientation

body.p: Collision hazards (R7). Clear the area at and below your altitude before any stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and keep clearing while you slow to lift-off speed [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The instructor should teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use before every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The AIM lists clearing before stalls, raising the wing in a high-wing airplane or lowering it in a low-wing airplane to look, and warns that the attitude of the aircraft creates additional blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Application: a power-on stall holds the nose high for a long time, hiding the sky ahead, so clear before the nose comes up.

The AIH reminds you why this is your job too: in one midair study a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the collisions, and most happened in daylight VFR. Any learner tendency to start a maneuver without checking for traffic must be corrected immediately [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Altitude (S2). Practice high enough to recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, or higher if the POH recommends [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Base it on the highest terrain and your airplane's own altitude loss. Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness and disorientation (R8):

bullets: Distractions: AC 61-67C's power-on stall plan has you distract the learner just before the stall and then discuss the effect [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200b]]. Most stall/spin accidents in the NTSB data happened when attention was diverted from flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Task prioritization: in a high-workload go-around, airplane control comes first; be careful reaching for the flap handle under high control pressures [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. On a short-field climb keep the eyes outside until obstacles are cleared [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

Loss of situational awareness: knowing position, flightpath and what comes next [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Losing it and not returning to the desired flightpath or following ATC instructions is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Disorientation: disoriented pilots may not be aware of their error, and many upsets happen while attention is on a task away from the instruments and outside references [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Recover with the outside horizon cross-checked against the attitude indicator.

callout.text: Application: give the lookout a job in the procedure. Before each stall, the learner calls 'clear left, clear right, clear below' and names one landmark to return to. The landmark doubles as the heading target for S10.

check.q: Why does a power-on stall need clearing completed before the nose comes up, more than many other maneuvers?
check.a: The AIM notes that the airplane's attitude creates additional blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], and the power-on entry holds the nose high for a long time, so clear at and below your altitude first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: On the checkride you demonstrate and explain at the same time. While demonstrating, the instructor explains the power settings, attitudes and other factors, in the same order as the briefing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Use the AFH procedure adjusted by your POH:

bullets: 1. Brief: impending or full, straight or turning, configuration, power, and the altitude, heading and airspeed to return to (AI.X.D.S8, S10). CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X: "the evaluator has discretion to ask for recovery at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall occurs", and "the applicant and the evaluator must review this area of operation during the preflight briefing."
2. Clear the area and confirm the altitude (AI.X.D.S1, S2) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Say: 'Clear left, clear right, nothing below; we will finish above 1,500 feet AGL.'

3. Set the configuration, then slow to lift-off speed holding altitude while still clearing [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.D.S3). Say: 'Takeoff flaps, slowing to lift-off speed so the nose will not be extreme.'

4. At lift-off speed set takeoff or recommended climb power, never below 65 percent, and establish the climb attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.D.S4). Say: 'Full power, right rudder coming in with it.'
5. For a turning stall, roll to the briefed bank of 15 to 20 degrees [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.D.S6).
6. Smoothly raise the nose and hold it, moving the elevator progressively back while adding right rudder [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.D.S5). Say: 'Back pressure growing, ball centered with right foot.'
7. Call the first cue (AI.X.D.S7). Impending: recover now. Full: hold the attitude until the full-stall cues [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
8. Recover: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinated, power confirmed [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (AI.X.D.S8).
9. Climb at VX or VY and configure as the manufacturer recommends (AI.X.D.S9) [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
10. Return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed (AI.X.D.S10).

head: Element
CFI ACS standard (AI.X.D)
rows: S2 Entry altitude
"Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL)" (ASEL)
S3 Configuration
"Establish the takeoff, departure, or cruise configuration, as specified by the evaluator, and maintain coordinated flight throughout the maneuver"
S4 Power
"Set power to no less than 65 percent power"
S5 Pitch
"Transition smoothly from the takeoff or departure attitude to the pitch attitude that induces a stall"
S6 Heading or bank

"Maintain a specified heading ±10° if in straight flight; maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±10° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall is reached, as specified by the evaluator"
S7 Cues
"Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)"
S8 Recovery
"Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator"
S9 Climb
Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY
S10 Return
"Return to the altitude, heading, and airspeed specified by the evaluator"

body.p: Note the bank tolerance. Power-on (AI.X.D.S6): "maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±10° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall is reached". Power-off (AI.X.C.S6): "maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±5° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall occurs". The 20° ceiling and the ±10° straight-flight heading tolerance are the same in both; only the bank tolerance differs.

callout.text: Application: talking while holding a nose-high attitude at full power is harder than it sounds. Practice the narration until the ball stays centered while you speak; an evaluator will notice a demo that drifts left every time you start a sentence.

check.q: In a turning power-on stall on the CFI checkride, the evaluator specifies 15 degrees of bank. What is the acceptable bank range until the stall, and how does that compare with the power-off Task?
check.a: 5 to 25 degrees: specified bank not to exceed 20 degrees, ±10° (AI.X.D.S6). The power-off Task allows only ±5° (AI.X.C.S6). The AFH uses 15 to 20 degrees of bank for power-on stalls [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: Ground first. Learning stalls through flight instruction alone goes slower than when the types and aerodynamics are discussed on the ground, and the task should be reviewed before flight even after ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For stalls, review the aerodynamics, then describe the physical sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. For this Task, the sensations to describe are the high nose, the heavy back pressure, the growing right rudder and a buffet that is stronger than in the power-off stall.
A building-block flow for power-on stalls (application of the simple-to-complex strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]):

bullets: 1. Slow flight first: note the left-turning tendency, the right rudder that centers the ball and holds heading, and the left yaw when the rudder is released [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]].
2. Impending power-on stalls straight ahead in takeoff configuration, then full stalls.
3. Turning stalls in both directions at 15 to 20 degrees of bank, then the clean configuration [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
4. Power-on stalls with a distraction just before the stall, then a talk about what it did to the entry and recovery [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200b]].
5. Tie it to the airplane's real departures: the elevator trim stall demonstration links it to go-arounds [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

body.p: Where the learner-tells step pays off in this Task: when the learner talks you through a power-on stall, you hear whether they think 'add power' is the fix. A misunderstanding can be corrected before the learner is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Bring it back to real takeoffs. On later flights do most of the teaching before calling the tower or announcing on the CTAF, and design takeoff scenarios, such as an imaginary obstacle, that do not lead the learner into an unsafe climb rate or excessive pitch attitude [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Practice the role yourself. The AIH's example has a CFI applicant brief and demonstrate stalls while another instructor plays an anxious learner, then critique the session [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. Do the same with a power-on stall before your checkride.

callout.text: Scenario-based training with realistic distractions helps protect pilots against a debilitating surprise or startle response [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Once the learner can fly a clean power-on stall, start it from a simulated go-around or obstacle climb instead of a 'now we will do a stall' call.

check.q: Before the first power-on stall, which slow flight demonstration from AC 61-67C sets up the rudder lesson, and what does it show?
check.a: Note the left-turning tendency, use right rudder to center the ball and hold heading, then release the rudder and have the learner watch the left yaw [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]].

chunks.title: Teaching safely: the learner who freezes or overcontrols

body.p: Anxiety shapes how a learner reacts at the break. Responses range from hesitancy to the urge to do something even if it is wrong; many freeze, and others act without rational thought [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. A learner reacting to stalls may go into fight or flight; you can take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage of an impending or full stall, and let them practice the stages until comfortable [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. A learner who feels unsafe focuses on fleeing, not on the skill [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

head: What the learner does
What you see in a power-on stall
What you do
rows: Freezes on the elevator
Nose stays high after the break, horn continuous, a wing starting to drop
Take the controls, calmly saying 'I have the flight controls', and recover [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Freezes off the rudder
Ball out to the right, nose sliding left as the speed decays
Prompt 'right rudder, center the ball' early; the yaw at the stall is what starts a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]
Overcontrols the entry
A yank, seat pressure, a sharp break at a higher speed than usual
An inadvertent accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; demonstrate a smooth, progressive raise of the nose [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Overcontrols the recovery
Objects float, learner lifts off the seat
Too much forward pressure gives low or negative G [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]; only enough to stop the warning
Startles
Sudden stiffening at the break or the horn
Startle is an automatic reflex [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]; brief the break so it is expected

bullets: Guard the controls: with hazardous maneuvers be ready to take control at any time, especially on a learner's first attempt [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and there is nothing to gain from fighting them for the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Your limits: never let a learner exceed your limits, and stay within your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Spins: practicing full stalls can result in inadvertent spins [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; you mitigate the risk by operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].
Pitch limit: review the POH for the airplane before you teach in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; some makers limit power-on stall pitch to 30 degrees [[24:347|AFH 17-13]].
Safety of flight: the applicant and the instructor or evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Application: decide on the ground the pitch attitude and bank at which you will take the controls, and tell the learner. A learner who knows the limit is less likely to freeze, and you are less likely to wait too long.

check.q: Your learner holds full back pressure after the break, the horn still blaring, and the left wing begins to drop. What does the AIH tell you to do?
check.a: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls'; anxious learners can be very strong and nothing is gained by fighting them for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Then reduce the AOA, level the wings and coordinate [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: The AFH lists 18 common errors in intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] and 10 in climbs and climbing turns [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. On the checkride the evaluator may play a learner and make them; you analyze and correct (AI.X.D.S11). The ones that show up most in power-on stalls:

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Inadvertent accelerated stall from pulling too fast on the power-on entry [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
A yank, seat pressure, an early sharp break
Raise the nose smoothly and hold the attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Allowing the airplane to yaw, usually from too little right rudder [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Ball right, nose sliding left
Right rudder grows as the speed decays [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Ball out as the nose drops and the speed builds
Fly the ball, not a fixed foot position [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
Climbing with one wing low from fixating on the nose [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Bank creeping in during a 'straight' stall
Use the wingtips as well as the nose for the climb attitude [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Not keeping a constant bank in turning stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Bank wanders as the nose rises
Set the bank first and hold it, coordinated, to the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Recovering with power before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Hand on the throttle, nose still high
Nose down first; power already in only reduces altitude loss [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Leveling the wings before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Aileron against the dropping wing, nose still high
Reduce AOA first, then roll [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]
Not holding nose-down input until the warning stops [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Back pressure returns with the horn on
Hold it until the stall warning is eliminated [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Inadvertent secondary stall during recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
A second buffet as the nose comes up
Let flying speed return before raising the nose [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
Excessive airspeed buildup [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Long dive at full power
Start the climb once speed is safe; reset the throttle [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Recovering before the critical AOA on a full stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Recovery at the first chirp when a full stall was asked for
Hold the attitude until the full-stall cues [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Losing situational awareness [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Wrong heading or altitude after the climb
Brief the return targets before the stall (AI.X.D.S10)

body.p: Decide whether the error is a misunderstanding or a lack of motor skill; having the learner think out loud makes the difference easy to see [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. 'I added power first because we were losing altitude' goes back to the ground brief. A late right foot needs more practice at slow flight power.

callout.text: Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out; a learner who rarely corrects an error learns the maneuver poorly [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In a power-on stall that margin is small, so set your take-over point first.

check.q: The 'learner' flies a straight-ahead power-on stall with the ball centered but the right wing slowly lowering, eyes fixed on the cowling. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Climbing with one wing low from fixation on the nose [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]; use the wingtips as well as the nose to set and hold the attitude [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

scenario.title: Power-on stalls on a hot afternoon with a nervous learner
scenario.setup: You are a CFI with a private pilot learner who has 18 hours. Today's lesson is the first power-on stalls, in a fixed-pitch, high-wing trainer with a stall horn. The field is at 2,400 ft MSL, it is 34 degrees C, the practice area terrain tops out at 2,900 ft MSL, and cumulus is building to the west. On the ramp the learner says their last instructor 'did one power-on stall and it rolled hard to the left', and they would rather skip it.

questions.q: How do you handle the learner's fear before you go?
questions.a: Treat it as normal: review the aerodynamics, describe the sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Offer to break the stall into stages you demonstrate one at a time, starting with impending stalls [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Explain that the hard roll was most likely yaw at the stall, which right rudder prevents [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and brief the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: What does the heat and elevation do to today's lesson?
questions.a: High density altitude reduces engine and propeller performance and climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], and normally aspirated engines lose power with altitude [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]; indicated stall speed hardly changes [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. Expect less power than at sea level and a slower climb back after each recovery. Check the POH that full throttle still gives at least 65 percent (AI.X.D.S4).

questions.q: What is the lowest altitude at which you will start each stall?
questions.a: High enough to finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL over the highest terrain, 2,900 + 1,500 = 4,400 ft MSL, plus your airplane's altitude loss in the recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] (AI.X.D.S2). And not below any cloud layer that would leave too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: Climbing to the practice area, the horn chirps once in a thermal bump during a VY climb. What do you teach from it?
questions.a: A vertical gust can raise the AOA suddenly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]; any stall warning should bring an instinctive response, lowering the nose since power is already in [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. It also shows the horn's small margin, typically 4 to 8 knots [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

questions.q: On the third stall the learner is busy with the clearing turn callouts and then the ball sits well right as the nose comes up. What do you do?
questions.a: Prompt right rudder early; yaw at the stall is what starts a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Insufficient right rudder letting the airplane yaw is a listed climb error [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. If the wing drops and the learner freezes, take the controls: 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: Coming back, the cumulus to the west now has a rain shaft and blowing dust near your departure path tomorrow. What is the lesson for the learner?
questions.a: Those are signs of a microburst [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On takeoff a microburst can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that drives the airplane toward the ground [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], and some cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. The defense is not departing under one.

skills.do: Clear the area at and below your altitude before slowing, and keep clearing while you slow to lift-off speed, explaining why the nose-high attitude makes clearing first important.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns with full callouts before every stall, and say aloud which part of the sky the raised nose will hide [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed "no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL)", and explain how you chose it.
skills.practice: Before each flight, add the highest terrain, 1,500 ft and your airplane's measured recovery loss on your kneeboard [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Establish the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration the evaluator specifies and stay coordinated throughout, explaining where the rudder demand comes from.
skills.practice: Practice in takeoff and clean configurations [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], calling the ball position every few seconds.

skills.do: Set power to "no less than 65 percent power" and explain why some airplanes use less than full power to limit the pitch attitude.
skills.practice: Find the RPM or manifold pressure for 65 percent in your POH for the day's altitude and temperature, and know the AFH reason for reduced power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Transition smoothly from the takeoff or departure attitude to the pitch attitude that induces a stall, while explaining why a quick pull is dangerous.
skills.practice: Have another CFI watch for any yank, the accelerated stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; count slowly as the nose comes up.

skills.do: "Maintain a specified heading ±10° if in straight flight; maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±10° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall is reached, as specified by the evaluator", without the narration pulling you off.
skills.practice: Fly turning stalls both ways at 15 to 20 degrees of bank [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] while talking, and check the heading indicator and attitude indicator at the break.

skills.do: Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall, such as buffet or the stall horn, out loud.
skills.practice: Name every cue as it appears, including RPM loss in a fixed-pitch airplane [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

skills.do: Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator, explaining why the AOA comes first even at full power.
skills.practice: Mix impending and full stalls each flight and read the request back before each one [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Rehearse the flap and gear sequence on the ground, then fly it, flaps up in increments at VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator specified.
skills.practice: Write the targets down before each stall; begin the level-off at about 10 percent of the climb rate [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors when the evaluator, acting as a learner, makes them: name the error, say what you saw, and give one fix.
skills.practice: Fly with another instructor who makes AFH-listed stall and climb errors on purpose [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and practice the one-line fix for each.

quiz.q: Which stall Tasks does CFI ACS Appendix 3 say the flight instructor normally demonstrates to learners for familiarization and stall/spin awareness?
options: Accelerated, secondary and power-on stalls
Power-off, power-on and accelerated stalls
Cross-controlled, elevator trim and secondary
Power-on, elevator trim and cross-controlled stalls
quiz.why: Appendix 3, Area X: "The flight instructor normally demonstrates stall Tasks F, G, and H to learners for the purposes of familiarization and stall/spin awareness": Task F cross-controlled, Task G elevator trim, Task H secondary. The AFH calls all three demonstration-only [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: From what flight conditions does the AFH have pilots practice power-on stall recoveries?
options: Steep climbing turns only, at 30 to 45 degrees of bank, full power
Straight glides and gliding turns of 30 degrees of bank
Level flight and level turns of 45 degrees of bank
Straight climbs and climbing turns of 15 to 20 degrees of bank
quiz.why: Power-on stall recoveries are practiced from straight climbs and climbing turns of 15 to 20 degrees of bank [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

quiz.q: In the PHAK sample stall speed table, gear and flaps up, wings level, what are the power-on and power-off stall speeds?
options: 57 knots power on, 47 knots power off
54 knots power on, 65 knots power off
47 knots power on, 57 knots power off
65 knots power on, 54 knots power off
quiz.why: Gear and flaps up, level: 54 knots power on, 65 knots power off [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Propeller slipstream lowers the power-on stall speed [[24:330|AFH 16-21]].

quiz.q: Why do the ailerons of most training airplanes keep some effect at the stall?
options: The tips are built with more camber, so they stall later
The ailerons sit in the full-power propeller slipstream
Wing fences hold the airflow attached out at the wingtips
Washout gives the tips a lower AOA, so the roots stall first
quiz.why: Most trainers have washout, so the wing roots pass the critical AOA before the tips and the ailerons keep some effect; still, reduce the AOA before rolling [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-67C, how much extra load factor does a stall entered from an unaccelerated straight climb produce?
options: About 1.4 G, since the nose is far above the horizon
None; only turns or abrupt pulls add load factor
About 2 G, the same as in a 60 degree banked turn
It depends on the power setting used for the climb
quiz.why: A stall entered from straight and level flight or from an unaccelerated straight climb will not produce additional load factors [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

quiz.q: In the AFH, what typically shows that a full stall, not just an impending stall, has occurred?
options: An uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested
A loss of RPM with a fixed-pitch propeller at full throttle
The first steady sound of the stall warning horn in the cockpit
Lighter control pressures and a slower response to inputs
quiz.why: Full stall indications are typically an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested, perhaps with an uncommanded roll; a horn is an impending-stall indication [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

quiz.q: Which of these does the AFH NOT list as a factor that affects an airplane's stall characteristics?
options: The outside air temperature
Its high-lift devices
Its center of gravity
The airplane's geometry
quiz.why: The AFH lists geometry, CG, wing design and high-lift devices [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

quiz.q: In the elevator trim stall demonstration, what two things make the nose rise sharply and turn left at full power?
options: Adverse yaw and a forward CG
Ground effect and propeller slip at the high power setting
Landing gear drag and a rapid flap retraction at low speed
Increased propwash over the tail and the nose-up trim
quiz.why: The combined effects of increased propwash over the tail and elevator trim make the nose rise sharply and turn left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH's NTSB figures, what share of stall/spin accidents occurred during takeoff and landing?
options: Sixty percent
Twenty percent
Eighty percent
Forty percent
quiz.why: Sixty percent of stall/spin accidents occurred during takeoff and landing, and twenty percent were preceded by engine failure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-67C, a spin that comes from crossed controls usually rotates in which direction?
options: Toward the raised wingtip, whichever wing that is
Opposite the rudder that is being applied
In the direction of the rudder applied
Always to the left in a trainer
quiz.why: The spin from cross-controlling usually rotates in the direction of the rudder being applied, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride the evaluator asks for a power-on stall in a high-performance single. At 65 percent power the nose would go past 30 degrees. What does the CFI ACS allow, and what does the AFH say about power?
options: Keep at least 65 percent and accept the pitch, since the ACS power line has no exceptions
Fly it at idle power instead, since that is the power-off Task's setting
Reduce power below the 65 percent guideline so the pitch stays at or under 30 degrees
Use full power but enter from cruise speed so the airplane reaches the stall sooner
final_quiz.why: CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task D: "In some high-performance airplanes, the power setting may have to be reduced below the ACS guidelines power setting to prevent pitch attitudes greater than 30° nose up." The AFH also says power may be reduced in some airplanes to prevent an excessively high pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: The 'learner' recovers from a full power-on stall by leaving the nose high and pushing the throttle against the stop, which is already full. The stall warning keeps sounding. What do you tell them?
options: Roll the wings level with aileron first, since a level wing will stop the stall warning
Hold the attitude a few more seconds until the extra power takes effect on the wing and breaks the stall
Add left rudder to stop the yaw first, then lower the nose once the wings are level
Power reduces altitude loss but never ends a stall; lower the nose until the warning stops
final_quiz.why: Adding power typically reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; reducing AOA is imperative [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Recovering with power before reducing AOA is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies a power-on stall with the ball centered until the nose drops, then the airplane yaws as the speed builds. What does the PHAK say about the left-turning forces that explains this?
options: They are set by the builder for climb speed, so they get stronger and stronger as the airplane speeds up
They grow larger as forward speed rises, since the propeller turns faster in a dive
Their values change with the flight condition, and the pilot must correct for whichever is strongest
They disappear completely the moment the stall warning stops, so no rudder is needed after
final_quiz.why: The four elements vary with flight situations, and the pilot must apply the controls to compensate for those varying values [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. The slipstream spiral weakens as forward speed increases [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

final_quiz.q: At the break your learner pushes the nose down but keeps both feet flat on the floor "to keep it simple", and the nose starts to yaw. What does the AFH recovery template say about rudder?
options: Proactively cancel yaw with rudder so the stall does not progress into a spin
Leave the rudder alone until the wings are level, then center the ball
Use rudder only if the cockpit placard says the airplane is approved for spins
Hold full right rudder until the airspeed is back to VY in the climb
final_quiz.why: Template step 3: proactively cancel yaw with proper use of the rudder to prevent a stall from progressing into a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The power-on recovery says coordinate with rudder [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: You plan the elevator trim stall demonstration. What does the CFI ACS require before you fly it, and what does the AFH say a full stall would cost?
options: Brief the recovery first; a full stall needs a big nose-down attitude and altitude loss
Brief only the entry; a full stall recovers by itself once the trim is reset nose-down
Nothing extra; full power is already set, so a full stall costs very little altitude
Brief the spin recovery; the full stall usually breaks into a spin to the right side
final_quiz.why: Appendix 3, Task G: "The applicant and evaluator must brief the recovery prior to stall execution." If taken to the full stall, recovery requires a significant nose-down attitude and a significant loss of altitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Before a learner's first full power-on stall you have briefed it and picked a take-over point. In flight, how does the AIH say the instructor mitigates the risk from the learner's actions?
options: By flying only impending stalls with a hand on the throttle
By letting the learner try them solo first, without pressure
Operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls
By waiting until the learner has passed the knowledge test
final_quiz.why: During flight instruction the instructor mitigates the risk of a learner's actions by operating at a safe altitude and by guarding the controls, then consciously accepts the risk that remains [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says, "Modern trainers won't spin, so the yaw in a power-on stall doesn't matter." What does the AFH say?
options: They cannot spin at all, because certification demands full spin resistance
They resist spins more, but mishandled controls can still spin them
They spin only with flaps extended, so a clean stall is safe from any yaw
They spin only at idle power, so the full-power stall cannot start a spin
final_quiz.why: Modern airplanes tend to be more reluctant to spin, but mishandling the controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can put even the most reluctant airplanes into an accidental spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: While teaching on a departure, you start explaining power-on stall theory during the takeoff roll. What does the AIH say about this?
options: It is ideal, since the learner is in the real situation and will remember it best
It is fine as long as the tower has not called you yet and the runway ahead is long
It helps if you speak louder than the engine and keep each of your points very short
Do most of the teaching before calling the tower or announcing, since the learner may not process it
final_quiz.why: There may not be time to teach during the takeoff; information may not be heard or processed, so do most of the teaching before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: A learner flying a turning power-on stall to the left lets the airplane skid with inside rudder and the stall breaks. Per AC 61-67C, which way will a spin from a skid rotate?
options: Opposite the aileron that is applied
In the direction the controls are applied
It depends only on the propeller direction
Toward the higher wingtip in most airplanes
final_quiz.why: In a skidding turn, with aileron and rudder applied the same way, rotation is in the direction the controls are applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner lifts off a short field in ground effect on a hot day, then pulls the nose up to clear trees while still below VX. What does the AFH say may happen?
options: The airplane will climb faster because ground effect lowers the drag
The airplane will accelerate quickly once it leaves the ground effect area
Ground effect makes the airplane stall at a lower angle of attack than usual
The airplane may not climb out of ground effect or clear obstructions
final_quiz.why: Climbing out of ground effect below the recommended speed gives much less climb; under high density altitude, temperature or weight the airplane may lift off but be unable to climb out of ground effect or clear obstructions [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, anxious about a hard wing drop on an earlier flight, freezes on every full power-on stall. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Fly only full stalls until the fear goes away, since repetition cures anxiety
Take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage, and let them practice the stages
Switch to accelerated stalls, since a sharper break will build their confidence
Stop teaching stalls and sign them off, since freezing will not happen solo
final_quiz.why: The instructor can take the procedure apart and demonstrate each stage of an impending or full stall, then let the learner practice the stages in realistic scenarios to build confidence [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

final_quiz.q: In a midair collision study the AIH cites, how often was a flight instructor on board?
options: In 57 percent of the accidents
In 7 percent of the accidents studied
In 37 percent of the accidents
In 77 percent of the accidents
final_quiz.why: Flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the accidents in the study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Clear before the nose comes up in a power-on stall.

final_quiz.q: After the power-on stalls, the "learner" wants to try accelerated stalls next without raising the takeoff flaps. What does the AFH say?
options: Fine, since flaps lower the stall speed and make the break much gentler
Never practice them with flaps extended, due to lower design G-load limits
Fine, as long as the airspeed stays above VA with the flaps still extended
Use full flaps instead, so the bank can stay below 30 degrees in the turn
final_quiz.why: A pilot should never practice accelerated stalls with wing flaps extended, due to the lower design G-load limitations in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

takeaways: A power-on stall rehearses departure accidents: nose too high after takeoff, in a climbing turn, over an obstacle or in a go-around.
Slow to lift-off speed before adding power so the nose is not held extremely high.
All four left-turning elements peak at high power and low speed; right rudder grows to the stall, then changes as the nose drops.
Power is already in, so the recovery is the nose: reduce AOA until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate, confirm power.
Watch for the power-on traps: a power-only recovery, a secondary stall, a long dive at full power and a yank on entry.
The CFI ACS bank tolerance here is ±10 degrees, not the ±5 of the power-off Task.
Brief your take-over point, guard the controls, and clear before the nose hides the sky.
cfi_notes: Sources differ on power. The CFI ACS asks for no less than 65 percent (AI.X.D.S4), and its Appendix 3 lets high-performance airplanes go lower to keep pitch at or below 30 degrees. The AFH single-engine text uses maximum power, reduced in some airplanes to avoid an excessively high pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Brief the POH setting and confirm it meets the ACS.

AC 61-67C (2000) says to apply maximum allowable power after reducing the AOA [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]; the newer AFH template adds power 'as needed' after the wings are level [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a power-on stall both end at the same throttle, but teach the AFH order.

The CFI ACS bank tolerance for turning power-on stalls is "±10° if in turning flight" (AI.X.D.S6); for power-off stalls it is "±5° if in turning flight" (AI.X.C.S6). Applicants who practiced only power-off stalls tend to assume one number for both.

The PHAK spells out the gyroscopic direction only for raising the tail (left yaw with a clockwise propeller) [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Applying it to the power-on stall recovery is this lesson's own reasoning, and no source says how large the effect is in a nosewheel trainer. Teach the AFH words instead: coordinate with rudder and cancel yaw [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

The AWH wind shear guidance is to keep or raise pitch and accept a lower airspeed [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]; the AFH says the most important action at an impending or full stall is to reduce AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The AWH cases involve airliners and stick shakers. Teach the stall recovery template at a stall warning and avoidance as the microburst defense.

The 4 to 8 knot warning margin is from AC 61-67C [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; 14 CFR 23.2150 gives no number [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. Have the learner note the horn speed and the stall speed in your airplane at full power.

Learners often over-learn 'right rudder' and keep holding it as the nose drops. Others under-learn it because the instructor's feet did the work in the demo. Take your feet off the pedals, visibly, after the first demonstration.

AC 61-67C's distraction should come just before the power-on stall [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200b]]. Pick one that keeps the learner's eyes partly outside, such as identifying a field, so you are not adding a collision risk to a nose-high maneuver.

The AIH lists the instructor as a hazard source in its own right: the learner on the controls may be a significant hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. In this Task that means deciding your take-over point before the stall, not during it.
gaps: No source gives the pitch attitude, power setting or 65 percent RPM for your trainer; use the POH/AFM power tables and limits.

Many POHs list only power-off stall speeds, and the airspeed arcs are power-off values [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]]. No source gives your airplane's power-on stall speed; measure it with your learner at altitude.
No source gives a light-airplane microburst escape procedure; the AWH cases are transport-category crews [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].
How hard a particular trainer drops a wing in an uncoordinated power-on stall, and how fast it spins, depends on the airplane and loading. A CFI experienced in the type is the best source.
The sources do not say how many power-on stalls a learner should fly before adding turns, the clean configuration or distractions; that is your judgment and the syllabus.

activities.title: Numbers for your power-on stall brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The PHAK power example uses an engine capable of 200 hp that needs only 130 hp for level flight. What percent of power is that, and is it enough for the CFI ACS power-on stall standard?
items.why: 130 / 200 = 0.65 = 65 percent [[1:262|PHAK 11-6]], exactly the "no less than 65 percent power" of AI.X.D.S4. Find the matching RPM in your POH.

items.q: PHAK sample table: gear and flaps up, power on, wings level stall speed is 54 knots. Many stall warning devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall. At the most, about what indicated speed might the horn first sound?
items.why: 54 + 8 = 62 knots (and 54 + 4 = 58 at the least) [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. A typical figure, not a promise for your airplane.

items.q: PHAK table, gear and flaps down, power on: 47 knots wings level and 66 knots at 60 degrees of bank. By about what percent does the stall speed rise? (AC 61-67C gives a figure for 60 degrees.)
items.why: 66 / 47 = 1.404, a rise of about 40 percent [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]], matching AC 61-67C: at 60 degrees of bank the load factor is 2 G and the stall speed rises 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]].

items.q: A microburst can produce downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm. At that rate, how many seconds would it take to lose 1,500 ft, the CFI ACS recovery floor above the ground?
items.why: 1,500 / 6,000 = 0.25 minute x 60 = 15 seconds [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]] (AI.X.D.S2). Avoid departing under a microburst.

items.q: AC 61-67C's rough estimate is about 500 ft lost per 3-second spin turn in most small airplanes approved for spins. How many seconds of spinning would use up 1,500 ft?
items.why: 1,500 / 500 = 3 turns x 3 seconds = 9 seconds [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Greater losses can be expected at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

activities.title: Which left-turning element is it?
activities.intro: Tap a description, then tap the element it belongs to.

items.t: Rolls the airplane opposite the direction the propeller turns
Older airplanes were rigged with more lift on the wing being forced down to fight it
Hits the vertical fin and is most compact at high propeller speed and low forward speed
Also makes a rolling moment to the right
A force on the propeller disc acts 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation
Best known when the tail is raised on a tailwheel takeoff roll
The downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite at a high AOA
Shrinks to zero when the propeller shaft is exactly aligned with the moving air

activities.title: True or false: cues and warnings at full power
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the PHAK, the spiraling slipstream becomes more compact and stronger as forward speed increases.
cards.why: False. As forward speed increases the spiral elongates and becomes less effective; it is most compact at high propeller speed and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: Once the nose is past 30 degrees up, the wing must be past its critical AOA.
cards.why: False. Attitude is not a reliable cue, since the airplane can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]; the critical AOA is fixed, not the pitch [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

cards.s: Under 14 CFR 23.2150 the stall warning must give at least 5 knots of margin.
cards.why: False. The rule requires a clear and distinctive warning with sufficient margin to prevent inadvertent stalling, and gives no number [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]].

cards.s: If incorrect rudder use created the yaw, the pilot may not know the critical AOA has been passed until the airplane yaws toward the lowering wing.
cards.why: True. If the yaw was created by incorrect rudder use, the pilot may not be aware the critical AOA has been exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

cards.s: AC 61-67C says a stall can occur at any power setting, including full power.
cards.why: True. A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any attitude, with any power setting [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100]].

cards.s: The AFH says the stall buffet in a level, coordinated turn can be sharper than in wings-level flight.
cards.why: True. An airplane typically stalls in a level, coordinated turn much as it does wings level, except that the stall buffet can be sharper [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

activities.title: CFI checkride: power-on stalls with the evaluator as your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant in the right seat. The evaluator plays a private pilot learner on a first power-on stall lesson and will make mistakes for you to catch.

steps.s: On the ground the "learner" briefs: "If the left wing drops at the break, I'll pick it up with right aileron, then lower the nose." What do you correct?
options: Nose down first: right aileron on the low wing raises its AOA and can deepen the stall
Use left aileron instead, since that lowers the AOA of the dropping wing
Add power first, so the ailerons get more slipstream before you roll
Nothing; leveling the wings first keeps the stall from becoming a spin
steps.why: The down aileron on the low wing raises its AOA and can make the tip stall more completely, rolling the airplane further; reduce the AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Leveling the wings before reducing AOA is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

steps.s: Clearing turns done, the "learner" slows toward lift-off speed for over a minute with eyes only on the airspeed indicator. What do you say?
options: Clearing is finished, so keep your eyes inside until after the stall and then look outside again
Good, the airspeed must be exact before you add power for the climb, so watch it the whole time
Skip it for now and do another pair of clearing turns after the stall once you are recovered
Keep clearing while you slow; the high nose will soon hide the sky ahead
steps.why: The pilot slows to lift-off speed while continuing to clear the area of other traffic [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], and the attitude of the aircraft creates additional blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

steps.s: Turning stall to the left: you specified 20 degrees of bank. At the break the "learner" is at 32 degrees. How do you critique it?
options: Within tolerance, since the ACS allows 20 degrees plus 15 in turns, so up to 35 degrees is acceptable
Out of tolerance: 20° ±10 allows 10 to 30 degrees, and bank must stay constant
Fine, since the AFH uses 30 to 45 degrees for climbing turn stalls, so 32 degrees is within range
Within tolerance, since the bank limit only applies before the stall and not at the moment of the break
steps.why: AI.X.D.S6: "maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±10° if in turning flight". Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; the AFH uses 15 to 20 degrees [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

steps.s: After the recovery, climbing at VY with takeoff flaps out, the "learner" reaches to raise all the flaps at once. What do you say?
options: Leave the flaps down until you are back at the assigned altitude, then raise them all in one motion
Good, raise them all at once now to cut the drag as fast as you can and speed up the climb out
Raise them in increments once stable at VY, to avoid a sudden loss of lift
Lower the nose to the horizon first, then raise them all at once as soon as the speed is building
steps.why: Once stabilized at VY, retract the flaps, usually in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]; a sudden and complete retraction could cause a loss of lift [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
